summary: Earth Jukebox makes NASA Earth science audible. It turns seven NASA Earth Information Center visualization sequences—near-surface temperature, wind, precipitation, specific humidity, PM2.5, ozone, and carbon monoxide—into browser-generated sound. Listeners can navigate with a keyboard and screen reader, choose the whole planet, a continent, or a country without relying on a mouse, move through frames, hear frame readings, and combine variables. An optional spoken guide for controls and a metronome support the listening experience. A jukebox-inspired interface gives each variable a distinct, repeatable sound mapping. The project offers blind and low-vision audiences another way to explore changing Earth patterns, while remaining open to everyone. The sounds follow documented rules applied to image-derived values; wind and PM2.5 use qualitative visual-signal indexes.
details:
Earth Jukebox turns seven NASA Earth Information Center visualization tracks into sound. The browser player decodes image colors using each visualization’s color scale, then maps image-derived values to musical notes, timbre, brightness, or rhythm using fixed rules. Tone.js synthesizes the sound live as the frames play.

Designed for keyboard navigation and screen readers, the experience lets listeners choose the whole planet, a continent, or a country without using a mouse. They can play or pause, move between frames, hear a frame’s readings, and combine variables in a separate mode. An optional spoken guide announces focused controls, and an optional metronome marks time intervals.

The jukebox concept turns Earth science into a collection of tracks to explore. It offers blind and low-vision audiences another way to engage with changing planetary patterns, while also inviting sighted visitors to listen.

The interface uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript ES modules. The offline image-processing and evaluation pipeline uses Python, NumPy, Pillow, Requests, scikit-image, SciPy, imageio-ffmpeg, and Matplotlib. Natural Earth country boundaries support geographic selections.

The team considered how to keep the sound mappings consistent across places and time, make the controls usable without a mouse, and avoid implying more scientific certainty than the image-derived values support. Wind and PM2.5 use qualitative visual-signal indexes; their sounds do not represent direct measurements of wind speed or pollutant concentration. AI tools assisted with selected coding, data analysis, research, and documentation tasks; the team chose the project concept and sound mappings.
